title: Learn Omarchy
description: Build practical desktop skills with guided shortcuts and real exercises. Optional modules let you explore further.

assisted.text: Nice work exploring this topic with some guidance. You can use Practice whenever you'd like to try the activities on your own.

explored.text: That's the end of this topic. You can revisit anything you skipped or want to practice, or choose another topic.

lessons.title: Welcome to Omarchy
lessons.description: Meet your coach and discover how to make this desktop your own. Replay the welcome anytime.

wrapUp.text: Nice work, that's the tour. You've explored the desktop bar, switched workspaces, and opened the Omarchy menu.

lessons.title: Omarchy tour
lessons.description: Get oriented with the desktop bar, try switching workspaces, then open the Omarchy menu.

steps.instruction: Let's start with the highlighted desktop bar. It gives you quick access to workspaces, the clock, and system controls. You'll use the Super key for many of Omarchy's keyboard shortcuts. On a Mac keyboard, that's Command. On a Windows keyboard, it's the Windows-logo key. When I say "hold Super," that's the key to use.
steps.detail: Follow the highlighted area if your bar is in a different position. Read along or listen, then press Enter to continue. Help can demonstrate shortcuts when you need it.

steps.instruction: These numbers are your workspaces: separate desktops for different tasks. The highlighted number shows the workspace you're using. Switching workspaces keeps your windows open.
steps.detail: Follow the highlighted area. Choose Next or press Enter when you're ready to continue.

steps.note: Your windows stay open when you switch workspaces.
steps.instruction: Hold Super and tap 2 on the top row. Then release both keys.
steps.detail: Switching workspaces doesn't close or move your windows. Workspace two may already have windows in it. If you're already there, we'll move on to switching to workspace one.
steps.completionMessage: You're on workspace two. Notice how its number is now highlighted in the bar. Your other windows are still on their own workspaces.

steps.instruction: Now hold Super and tap 1 on the top row. Then release both keys. You're heading to workspace one.
steps.detail: If you started on workspace one, this brings you back. If you started elsewhere, it takes you to workspace one instead. Nothing is closed or moved.
steps.completionMessage: You're on workspace one. You can use the same shortcut whenever you want to switch workspaces. Let's continue along the bar.

steps.instruction: Here's the date and time, with weather alongside it if enabled. The clock opens a calendar. Hovering over this area can also reveal quick tools, including reminders and screen recording.
steps.detail: Follow the highlighted area. Choose Next or press Enter when you're ready to continue.

steps.instruction: These indicators show system status, including network, Bluetooth, sound, and power. Select an indicator to open its controls. What you see depends on your hardware and bar settings.
steps.detail: Follow the highlighted area. Choose Next or press Enter when you're ready to continue.

steps.instruction: Let's try another shortcut. Hold Super and tap Space to open the Omarchy menu.
steps.detail: The Omarchy menu brings together apps, settings, and system tools. In guided activities, the course captures your shortcut keys; Release Keys lets you interact with the opened menu.
steps.completionMessage: That's the Omarchy menu in the center of your screen. It brings together apps, settings, and system tools. Super and Space opens it whenever you need it.

steps.instruction: You can also click this icon in the desktop bar to open the same menu, with apps, settings, and other resources. Use whichever way is more convenient.
steps.detail: The previous menu is closed so you can see the icon clearly. This is the mouse alternative to Super and Space; you don't need to click it to finish the tour.

wrapUp.text: That wraps up menus and apps. You have a starting point for finding commands, opening apps, and looking up shortcuts.

lessons.title: Menus and apps
lessons.description: Find commands, installed apps, and the built-in shortcut guide.

steps.instruction: Press Super and Space to open the Omarchy menu. If you tried this on the tour, use it as a quick refresher or choose Skip.
steps.detail: This menu is a useful starting point for apps, settings, and system tools.
steps.completionMessage: The menu is open. Choose Release Keys before typing or browsing here. Escape closes the menu; Capture Keys returns control to the course.

steps.instruction: Now for your apps. Alt is the Option key on a Mac keyboard. Hold Super and Alt, then tap Space to open the Apps menu.
steps.detail: The Apps menu lists launchable apps, not every installed package. Choose Release Keys to search it, then Capture Keys to return to the course.
steps.completionMessage: The Apps menu is open. The next exercise lets you search for and launch an app yourself.

steps.note: The exercise opens separately and gives you control of the keyboard.
steps.instruction: Now use the Apps menu for a real task. Search for your terminal, launch it, then close that new window.
steps.detail: Start exercise releases the keys to a normal desktop window. Follow its instructions, then choose Finish exercise to return here.
steps.completionMessage: You opened the menu, launched a new terminal, and closed that window. Searching the Apps menu is a useful way to find an app when you don't know its shortcut.

steps.instruction: Need to look up a shortcut? Press Super and K to open the shortcut guide.
steps.detail: This searchable list is your cheat sheet. Choose Release Keys to type a filter. Close the guide with Escape, then choose Capture Keys to continue.
steps.completionMessage: The shortcut guide is open. Use it whenever you want to look up or revisit a key combination.

wrapUp.text: Nicely done. You've practiced opening everyday apps and closing the windows you no longer need.

lessons.title: Everyday apps
lessons.description: Launch the terminal, browser, and file manager, and learn to close what you open.

steps.note: A terminal is a window where you can type commands.
steps.instruction: Press Super and Return to open a terminal. Return is the Enter key on most keyboards.
steps.detail: A terminal is a window where you can type commands. You won't need to enter commands in this activity. Omarchy fits the new window alongside your existing work.
steps.completionMessage: That's your terminal, one shortcut away from anywhere in Omarchy.

steps.note: Only the terminal opened for this activity will close.
steps.instruction: Now let's tidy up. Press Super and W to close that terminal.
steps.detail: Outside the course, this closes the active window: the one receiving your input. Here, the guided action targets only the terminal opened for this activity.
steps.completionMessage: The practice terminal is closed. Super and Return opens one; Super and W closes the active window.

steps.instruction: Let's get online. Hold Super and Shift, then press Return to open your browser.
steps.detail: This shortcut uses the browser you've configured in Omarchy. Browser settings can affect whether a new window opens.
steps.completionMessage: Your browser is ready. Super, Shift, and Return is the shortcut to remember.

steps.note: A file manager helps you browse folders and documents.
steps.instruction: Need your files? Hold Super and Shift, then press F to open the file manager.
steps.detail: The file manager opens in a new window, ready for browsing, drag and drop, or a quick search.
steps.completionMessage: The file manager is open. Use it to browse folders, find documents, and manage files.

steps.note: Your other windows stay open.
steps.instruction: Same move again. Press Super and W to close the file manager.
steps.detail: The guided action closes the course's file-manager window, not another window you had open.
steps.completionMessage: The file manager is closed. You can keep the browser open or close it when you're finished with it.

wrapUp.text: Nice work. You've practiced arranging windows and switching your focus between them. Use the layout that suits your task.

lessons.title: Windows
lessons.description: Tile, focus, float, and fullscreen windows without touching the mouse.

steps.note: Tiling arranges your windows without overlap.
steps.instruction: Let's see how tiling works. Press Super and Return to open a terminal.
steps.detail: Tiling arranges windows without overlap. A single tiled window fills the available workspace; additional windows share that space.
steps.completionMessage: The terminal has joined your layout. Next, open another to see how the available space is shared.

steps.instruction: Press Super and Return once more to open a second terminal.
steps.detail: Tiling means no overlapping and no manual arranging. Omarchy splits the space for you.
steps.completionMessage: There's your second practice terminal. Omarchy fits it around any windows you already had open.

steps.note: Focus means which window receives your keyboard input.
steps.instruction: Two windows, one keyboard. Press Alt and Tab to hop to the other terminal.
steps.detail: Focus means which window receives keyboard input. Alt and Tab switches windows; the active border helps you spot the change. This guided step selects your other practice terminal.
steps.completionMessage: The other terminal now receives your keyboard input. You can switch between windows without moving them.

steps.note: Floating windows can sit above the tiled layout.
steps.instruction: Sometimes you want a window to float free. Press Super and T to toggle floating.
steps.detail: A floating window sits on top of the tiles and can be dragged around with Super and the mouse. Press Super and T again to tile it back.
steps.completionMessage: It's floating now. Handy for a calculator or a chat window you want to keep in view.

steps.note: Use the same shortcut again to leave fullscreen.
steps.instruction: Need to focus on one thing? Press Super and F for fullscreen.
steps.detail: Super+F toggles fullscreen. You'll press the same shortcut again in the next activity to get your desktop back.
steps.completionMessage: The terminal is fullscreen. Press the same shortcut in the next activity to leave fullscreen.

steps.instruction: Press Super and F again to leave fullscreen.
steps.detail: The same shortcut gets you in and out, so you're never stuck.
steps.completionMessage: Fullscreen is off. You can return to the bar and your other windows.

steps.instruction: Press Super and T to put that floating terminal back into the tiled layout.
steps.detail: Tiling fits the practice window around your existing work.
steps.completionMessage: Your terminal is tiled again. Omarchy manages its size and position alongside the other windows.

steps.instruction: Super and an arrow focuses a neighboring window. Use the highlighted arrow to focus your other practice terminal.
steps.detail: The arrow follows your terminals' actual positions. This guided action doesn't change any of your existing windows.
steps.completionMessage: Your second terminal has focus. Directional shortcuts save you from cycling through every window.

steps.note: Only our two practice terminals will change positions.
steps.instruction: Add Shift to swap window positions. Hold Super and Shift, then press the highlighted arrow.
steps.detail: Outside the course this swaps with the neighboring window. Here we safely exchange only our two practice terminals.
steps.completionMessage: Your practice terminals traded places. Adding Shift changes directional focus into a window swap.

steps.instruction: Let's clean up. Press Super and W to close this window.
steps.detail: Closing a tiled window gives its space back to the others instantly.
steps.completionMessage: The first practice terminal is closed. The remaining windows can use the space it released.

steps.instruction: And once more. Press Super and W to close the last terminal.
steps.detail: That's the whole loop: open, arrange, focus, close. All from the keyboard.
steps.completionMessage: Both practice terminals are closed. You've covered opening, arranging, switching between, and closing windows.

wrapUp.text: That wraps up workspaces. You can keep different tasks on separate desktops and switch between them without closing your windows.

lessons.title: Workspaces
lessons.description: Jump between desktops, send windows where they belong, and stash things in the scratchpad.

steps.instruction: First, let's start from workspace one. Press Super and 1.
steps.detail: If you're already on workspace one, this step takes care of itself.
steps.completionMessage: You're on workspace one. We'll use it as the starting point for this lesson.

steps.instruction: We'll need a window to move around. Press Super and Return to open a terminal.
steps.detail: Workspaces are separate desktops. Each one holds its own set of tiled windows.
steps.completionMessage: The practice terminal is open. Watch the workspace numbers as you move between desktops.

steps.note: Your windows stay open when you switch workspaces.
steps.instruction: Press Super and 2 to visit workspace two.
steps.detail: Workspaces separate your tasks. A workspace may already contain windows; switching doesn't close them.
steps.completionMessage: You're on workspace two. Anything you already had here stays in place.

steps.instruction: Press Super, Control, and Tab to return to the workspace you were just using.
steps.detail: This shortcut returns to the last workspace you visited. In this activity, that's workspace one.
steps.completionMessage: And you're back. Now let's move the terminal instead of ourselves.

steps.note: The terminal moves to workspace two, and you follow it.
steps.instruction: Hold Super and Shift, then press 2 to send this terminal to workspace two.
steps.detail: Super, Shift, and a number moves the focused window to that workspace and follows it there.
steps.completionMessage: The terminal is now on workspace two, and you've followed it there. Moving a window lets you keep related work together.

steps.instruction: Let's hop desktops. Press Super and Tab to move to the next workspace.
steps.detail: Workspaces keep projects separate without minimizing anything. Watch the numbers in the bar.
steps.completionMessage: See the highlight move in the bar? That's you on a new workspace.

steps.instruction: Now head back. Hold Super and Shift, then press Tab to return to the previous workspace.
steps.detail: Adding Shift reverses the direction. Super plus a number jumps straight to that workspace.
steps.completionMessage: You're back on the previous workspace. Shift reverses the direction of this shortcut.

steps.note: The scratchpad is a hidden workspace you can show over your desktop.
steps.instruction: Let's give the scratchpad something useful. Press Super, Alt, and S to put our terminal there.
steps.detail: The scratchpad is a temporary workspace you can reveal over your current one. Your other windows aren't moved.
steps.completionMessage: The terminal is in the scratchpad. Next, reveal it over your current workspace.

steps.instruction: Press Super and S to reveal the scratchpad with your terminal in it.
steps.detail: The scratchpad is a hidden workspace you can show over your current one. Super and S shows or hides it.
steps.completionMessage: There's your terminal, available without leaving this workspace.

steps.note: The terminal stays open while the scratchpad is hidden.
steps.instruction: Press Super and S again to tuck the scratchpad away.
steps.detail: Anything you leave in the scratchpad stays there until you call it back.
steps.completionMessage: The scratchpad is hidden, but its terminal is still open. We'll reveal it again before moving the terminal to a numbered workspace.

steps.note: Select our practice terminal if other windows are in the scratchpad.
steps.instruction: Reveal the scratchpad again with Super and S. We'll move the practice terminal only after it has focus.
steps.detail: If the scratchpad contains other windows, select the terminal we opened. The next shortcut moves the focused window, not a window hidden in the scratchpad.
steps.completionMessage: The practice terminal is visible and focused. Now you can move it out of the scratchpad.

steps.note: The terminal must be visible and focused before you move it.
steps.instruction: Press Super, Shift, and 2 to bring the practice terminal back to workspace two.
steps.detail: The terminal must be visible and focused. Sending it to a numbered workspace takes it out of the scratchpad.
steps.completionMessage: The terminal is back on workspace two and no longer in the scratchpad.

steps.instruction: Let's leave the desktop tidy. Press Super and W to close our practice terminal.
steps.detail: This guided action closes only the terminal from this lesson. Your other work stays open.
steps.completionMessage: The practice terminal is closed. You've moved between workspaces, moved a window, and used the scratchpad.

wrapUp.text: You've explored the desktop controls. The bar gives you a quick place to check your system and reach the settings you need.

lessons.title: Desktop controls
lessons.description: Optional: understand status, preview themes, and explore desktop controls safely.

steps.note: Output is where sound plays; input is your microphone.
steps.instruction: Hold Super and Control, then press A to open the Audio panel.
steps.detail: Output is where sound plays; input is your microphone. Release Keys to explore the panel, Escape to close it, then Capture Keys to return. No volume changes are required.
steps.completionMessage: The Audio panel shows volume and sound devices. You don't need to change any settings for this activity.

steps.note: Check the connection without disconnecting or changing networks.
steps.instruction: Hold Super and Control, then press W to open the Network panel.
steps.detail: Read the connection status without disconnecting. Release Keys to use the panel, Escape to close it, and Capture Keys to return.
steps.completionMessage: The Network panel is open. You can check your connection without disconnecting or changing networks.

steps.instruction: How's your battery? Hold Super and Control, then press P to open the Power panel.
steps.detail: Battery status and power profiles, ready for when you need to squeeze out more time.
steps.completionMessage: Battery and power profiles, all at a glance.

steps.note: Clicking the clock opens the same calendar.
steps.instruction: What's the date? Hold Super, Control, and Alt, then press D to open the calendar.
steps.detail: Clicking the clock is a useful alternative to this longer shortcut. Explore with Release Keys; Escape closes the panel.
steps.completionMessage: There's your calendar, the same view you get by clicking the clock.

steps.note: Choosing a background changes your desktop immediately.
steps.instruction: Fancy a new look? Hold Super and Control, then press Space to open the Background switcher.
steps.detail: Opening this preview doesn't apply anything. Release Keys to browse; Escape cancels. Applying a selection is optional and changes your desktop immediately. Remember your current choice so you can return to it.
steps.completionMessage: Pick a background you like, or press Escape to keep the one you have.

steps.note: Choosing a theme applies it immediately; no change is required.
steps.instruction: Hold Super, Shift, and Control, then press Space to open the Theme menu.
steps.detail: Opening this preview doesn't apply anything. Release Keys to browse; Escape cancels. Applying a selection is optional and changes your desktop immediately. Remember your current choice so you can return to it.
steps.completionMessage: Themes coordinate the desktop's appearance. Selecting one applies a change; close the menu without choosing to keep your current theme.

steps.note: Selecting an entry changes that setting.
steps.instruction: One more. Hold Super and Control, then press O to open the Toggle menu.
steps.detail: Night light, idle locking, the top bar, and other switches all live here.
steps.completionMessage: The Toggle menu is open. Selecting an entry changes that setting; closing the menu alone doesn't undo changes you've made.

wrapUp.text: Nicely done. You've explored clipboard history and practiced Compose sequences. A few useful characters and shortcuts can save you time.

lessons.title: Clipboard and Compose
lessons.description: Retrieve older clipboard entries and type emojis with sequential Compose keys.

steps.instruction: Omarchy provides shared copy and paste shortcuts: Super and C to copy, and Super and V to paste. They work across supported apps, including the terminal, where the usual shortcuts can differ.
steps.detail: Select text before copying, then choose where to paste it. Custom bindings and individual apps can affect these shortcuts.

steps.note: History may contain private information; select entries carefully.
steps.instruction: Copied something earlier? Hold Super and Control, then press V to open your clipboard history.
steps.detail: Clipboard history keeps recent copied items. Activating an entry normally pastes it into the previously focused field. Shift+Enter copies an entry without pasting. Be mindful of private information in your history.
steps.completionMessage: Clipboard history is open. After releasing the keys, select an entry and use Shift and Enter to copy it without pasting. Regular Enter pastes into the previous field.

steps.note: This exercise replaces your clipboard with harmless sample text.
steps.instruction: Let's make clipboard history useful. Copy two sample notes. Find the older one in history, use Shift and Enter to copy it without pasting, then paste it into the exercise.
steps.detail: The exercise uses harmless text, but it replaces the current clipboard. Keys go to the exercise window until you finish or close it.
steps.completionMessage: You retrieved an older clipboard entry and pasted it. That's useful when a newer copy replaces something you still need.

steps.instruction: Caps Lock has a second job in Omarchy: it's the Compose key. Tap and release Caps Lock, then m, then s for a smile. These are separate presses, not a shortcut you hold together.
steps.detail: Compose uses separate key presses, not keys held together. Use lowercase letters without Shift. We'll practice a smile and a heart next. Custom keyboard settings may use a different Compose key.

steps.note: Custom Compose settings may differ; skipping is fine.
steps.instruction: Let's type a smile and a heart without opening the emoji picker. Follow the keys in order, one at a time.
steps.detail: The normal text field receives Compose input. The exercise checks the resulting emojis. If Caps Lock has been remapped, use the picker in everyday work and skip this exercise rather than changing your keyboard settings.
steps.completionMessage: Two little sequences, two emojis. That's Compose: tap the keys in order, instead of holding a chord.

wrapUp.text: That wraps up capture. You've practiced making a screenshot and a short recording. Remember to check for private information before sharing.

lessons.title: Capture
lessons.description: Capture an image, record and replay a short clip, and optionally extract text or decode a QR code.

steps.instruction: Grab what's on screen. Hold Super and Control, then press C to open the Capture menu.
steps.detail: Screenshots, screen recordings, color picking, and text extraction all start here.
steps.completionMessage: Screenshots, recordings, and more, all from one menu.

steps.instruction: To take a screenshot, press Print. No Print key? Search Screenshot in the Omarchy menu instead. Drag over the area you want to capture. Escape cancels.
steps.detail: The native picker freezes the screen. Tab selects a window and Enter captures it; Control+Enter captures the whole screen. Screenshots save to your configured Pictures directory and clipboard. Click the screenshot notification to edit it, or use Super+Alt+Comma while it's the latest actionable notification. Avoid private content before capturing.

steps.note: Capture only the sample card, not private windows or notifications.
steps.instruction: Capture the practice card, inspect the saved image, copy its file path, and add a label to the preview.
steps.detail: Only capture the sample card, not private windows or notifications. The exercise uses its own capture tools. Preview labels don't alter the saved image, and nothing is uploaded.
steps.completionMessage: You've captured and reviewed an image, copied its path, and labeled the preview. The saved image itself is unchanged.

steps.instruction: Alt and Print opens recording choices, or stops a recording that's already running. Without a Print key, use the Capture menu. Watch the recording indicator, and make sure you know how to stop before starting.
steps.detail: Native recordings go to your configured Videos directory. No audio, desktop audio, microphone, and webcam are different choices. Never include someone else's voice, private windows, or notifications without permission. Our practice recording is silent and limited to a region you choose.

steps.note: Review the selected region; no microphone or webcam is enabled.
steps.instruction: Let's make a short, silent recording of the practice card. Start explicitly, stop it yourself, then play the saved clip.
steps.detail: No microphone or webcam is enabled. The exercise owns only its recorder and output. It must not stop an existing recording. Review the selected region before starting.
steps.completionMessage: You started, stopped, and replayed a real recording. Knowing how to stop is just as important as knowing how to start.

steps.note: OCR turns images into text; check the result for mistakes.
steps.instruction: An image can contain useful text. Select the sample text on the practice card, extract it, and paste the result.
steps.detail: OCR means optical character recognition. Outside the course, Super+Ctrl+Print opens text capture. Recognition can make mistakes, so compare the pasted words with the original. This optional exercise uses only a harmless sample.
steps.completionMessage: You turned pixels into editable text. Give extracted text a quick proofread before you use it.

steps.note: Our sample contains harmless text; no website will open.
steps.instruction: Let's read a QR code that's already on screen. Capture the sample code, then paste the decoded text.
steps.detail: Search QR Code in the Omarchy menu for the everyday tool. Our sample contains harmless text, not a website. Decoding a QR code isn't a reason to open an unfamiliar link automatically.
steps.completionMessage: You've read the QR code without reaching for your phone, and checked its contents before acting.

wrapUp.text: You've explored where to find apps and upkeep tools. Knowing where a setting lives is a useful first step. Read the changes before confirming them.

lessons.title: Apps and upkeep
lessons.description: Find install, removal, defaults, updates, and recovery tools without changing the system.

steps.instruction: Search Install in the Omarchy menu. Just note the location; don't install anything for this lesson. A package is installable software. Prefer official packages. Community packages from the Arch User Repository, or AUR, need closer review.
steps.detail: This is an introduction, not an installation task. Use Release Keys if you'd like to locate Install, then Escape and Capture Keys to return. Installing software can request your password and change the system. No installation is required for completion.

steps.instruction: The Remove menu uninstalls software you no longer need. Before confirming, check the package name and any other software it would remove. There's nothing to uninstall in this lesson.
steps.detail: A dependency is software another app needs. Explore the menu if useful, but cancel before removing anything.

steps.instruction: Setup, Defaults is where you choose which apps Omarchy opens. For now, just note the location; keep your current settings. Installing an app and making it the default are separate decisions.
steps.detail: Open Super+Space, then search Defaults. Selecting a default changes future launches immediately. This lesson only introduces the location; keep your current defaults unless you intentionally want to change them.

steps.instruction: The Update menu keeps Omarchy and its packages current. We're not running an update in this lesson. When you do update, save your work first and read the proposed changes. Stay on the stable channel for everyday use.
steps.detail: Some installations create filesystem snapshots before updates, allowing system changes to be rolled back. A snapshot isn't an independent backup of your personal files. This lesson doesn't run an update.

steps.instruction: If one device stops working, Update, Hardware offers targeted restarts. Just note the location for now; don't restart anything during this lesson. Resetting configuration is different from updating and can replace your custom settings.
steps.detail: Your user settings generally live under ~/.config; packaged Omarchy defaults live under /usr/share/omarchy and shouldn't be edited. Back up your changes before resets. Restarting network or audio services can interrupt active calls, downloads, and recordings, so this lesson performs none.

wrapUp.text: That wraps up setup and system controls. You know where to look when you need them, without changing settings just for practice.

lessons.title: Setup and system
lessons.description: Reach hardware setup, display settings, and safe system actions from the keyboard.

steps.instruction: Let's look under the hood. Hold Super and Control, then press H to open the Hardware menu.
steps.detail: Audio, Bluetooth, display, keyboard, and other device settings gather here.
steps.completionMessage: Hardware setup lives here. Install and Update are one level up, in the Omarchy menu under Super plus Space.

steps.note: Display changes apply immediately; leave resolution and scale unchanged.
steps.instruction: Hold Super and Control, then press D to open the Display panel.
steps.detail: Display changes apply immediately. Read the panel without changing scale or resolution during this lesson. Release Keys to explore; Escape closes it.
steps.completionMessage: The Display panel is open. Resolution and scaling changes apply immediately, so leave them unchanged unless you intend to adjust your display.

steps.note: Close the menu without choosing logout, restart, or shutdown.
steps.instruction: Hold Super and press Escape to open the System menu.
steps.detail: Lock, suspend, log out, reboot, or shut down from one keyboard-driven list.
steps.completionMessage: The System menu is open. Close it without selecting an action to keep working; actions such as logout or shutdown can interrupt your session.

steps.note: Locking is optional; save your work and know your password first.
steps.instruction: Build one useful habit: Super, Control, and L locks your screen. Practice only when you're ready.
steps.detail: This optional exercise won't lock anything until you explicitly choose Lock this computer now. You'll need your password to return. Skipping it doesn't block the lesson.
steps.completionMessage: You've locked the computer and returned after unlocking it. Use that shortcut when you step away.

wrapUp.text: That wraps up productivity extras. You've explored emojis, reminders, and dictation. Choose the tools that help with your own work.

lessons.title: Productivity extras
lessons.description: Optional: the emoji picker, reminders, local dictation, and word corrections.

steps.note: The selected emoji is inserted into your previous text field.
steps.instruction: Need an emoji? Hold Super and Control, then press E to open the emoji picker.
steps.detail: Type a word to search, press Enter, and the emoji lands in whatever you were typing.
steps.completionMessage: There they all are. Search, Enter, done. No more hunting through menus.

steps.note: Scheduling a reminder is optional; Escape cancels.
steps.instruction: Need a reminder? Hold Super and Control, then press R to set one.
steps.detail: Enter the number of minutes first, then your reminder message. Press Escape to leave without scheduling anything.
steps.completionMessage: The reminder prompt is open. You can set a timed reminder or close it without scheduling one.

steps.note: You control the microphone; skip if dictation isn't available.
steps.instruction: If local dictation is installed, try speaking into a text field. Super, Control, and X starts and stops dictation, so you don't need an F9 key. You control the microphone.
steps.detail: You can also hold F9 for push-to-talk with Voxtype. The exercise checks availability and the sample text you enter and review, not whether dictation produced it. It doesn't start your microphone. Skip if dictation isn't available.
steps.completionMessage: You've explored local dictation and its controls. Always check recognized words before sending a message.

steps.instruction: Names and technical words can trip up speech recognition. Voxtype's replacement settings let you correct recurring mistakes. Keep replacements specific so an ordinary word doesn't unexpectedly turn into something else.
steps.detail: Find dictation setup in the Omarchy menu. Review the installed tool's configuration before editing, save a backup, and test with a harmless phrase. This introduction doesn't edit replacement rules or claim they affect every kind of typing.

wrapUp.text: That wraps up useful tools. You have places to check resource use, do a quick calculation, and investigate disk space before deleting anything.

lessons.title: Useful tools
lessons.description: Optional: inspect resource use, open the calculator, and learn safe disk-usage inspection.

steps.note: Inspect resource use without stopping any programs.
steps.instruction: Wondering what's using your computer? Press Super, Control, and T to open the activity monitor.
steps.detail: The activity monitor shows processor use, memory, storage, and running programs. Release Keys to explore, then Capture Keys to return. Don't stop any programs for this lesson.
steps.completionMessage: The activity monitor is open. Use it to understand resource use before deciding whether anything needs attention.

steps.instruction: Press Super and W to close our activity monitor.
steps.detail: The course closes only the window it opened, never an existing tool window.
steps.completionMessage: Closed. Your other work stays where you left it.

steps.note: The lesson checks that the calculator opens, not your calculation.
steps.instruction: For a quick calculation, press Super, Control, and Q. The calculator is built right in.
steps.detail: Release Keys and try 5 + 5, then Capture Keys to return. This activity checks that the calculator opened, not the calculation. An existing calculator window won't be closed by the course.
steps.completionMessage: The calculator is open. You can try a calculation before returning to the lesson.

steps.instruction: Press Super and W to close our calculator.
steps.detail: The course closes only the window it opened, never an existing tool window.
steps.completionMessage: Closed. Your other work stays where you left it.

steps.instruction: Running low on space? Search Disk Usage in the Omarchy menu to see where it's going. Inspect before deleting: a large folder might be important work, not disposable clutter.
steps.detail: This is a read-only introduction. Don't use trash or permanent-delete commands as part of the lesson. Backups, application caches, and system packages need different cleanup decisions.

wrapUp.text: Nice work exploring these creation and sharing tools. Preview what you've made, and check the file and recipient before sending anything.

lessons.title: Create and share
lessons.description: Optional: web-app launchers, smaller video files, and safe LocalSend preparation.

steps.note: This local demo doesn't change your Apps menu.
steps.instruction: A web app gives a website its own launcher. Create a local demo entry, preview it, then remove it. This practice doesn't add anything to your Apps menu.
steps.detail: In everyday Omarchy, Install Web App asks for a name and website address; Remove Web App removes its launcher. This exercise uses a temporary local preview and makes no network request.
steps.completionMessage: A web app is a launcher for a site, not a separate account or a replacement for the browser's security.

steps.note: Transcoding converts media; your original file is kept.
steps.instruction: A recording can be too large to share comfortably. Let's create a smaller copy of a harmless practice clip and inspect the result.
steps.detail: Transcoding means converting media. Keep the original, choose a sensible resolution, and compare the output before sharing. MP4 suits longer clips; GIF can be convenient for short, silent loops but isn't always smaller.
steps.completionMessage: You've created a separate output and kept the original. Check quality and size before you share it.

steps.note: Opening the menu sends nothing; check the file and recipient before sharing.
steps.instruction: Here's an optional tool for sharing. Press Super, Control, and S to open the Share menu.
steps.detail: Opening the menu sends nothing. Before sharing, check the selected content and recipient. Never send secrets or personal files just to complete a lesson. Escape cancels.
steps.completionMessage: The Share menu is open. Sending anything is optional and always your decision.

steps.note: This rehearsal doesn't discover devices or send anything.
steps.instruction: LocalSend shares files with nearby devices. In this rehearsal, review a sample file and choose an intended demo recipient. Nothing will be sent.
steps.detail: Real transfers need LocalSend on both devices and a network connection between them. Check both the file and recipient before sending. This exercise doesn't discover devices or confirm delivery.
steps.completionMessage: You reviewed the safe sharing workflow. Delivery to another device is a separate action that this course doesn't assume.

wrapUp.text: Nicely done. You've brought app, window, and workspace shortcuts together in one workflow. Super and K opens the shortcut guide whenever you need a reminder. Keep the shortcuts that help you. Your desktop. Your way.

lessons.title: Your first real session
lessons.description: Combine app, window, and workspace shortcuts in one practical workflow.

steps.instruction: Bring the shortcuts together in a short workflow: open a terminal and browser, move the browser to another workspace, then close both. Use Help whenever you need a reminder.
steps.detail: Use your existing desktop. We'll verify only the windows opened by this lesson and leave your other work alone.

steps.instruction: Let's begin on workspace one. Press Super and 1.
steps.detail: If you're already on workspace one, this step takes care of itself.
steps.completionMessage: Good. Everything starts from here.

steps.instruction: Start with a terminal. Press Super and Return.
steps.completionMessage: Terminal's up.

steps.instruction: Now a browser. Hold Super and Shift, then press Return.
steps.completionMessage: Both practice windows are open. Next, give the browser its own workspace.

steps.instruction: Let's give the browser its own desktop. Hold Super and Shift, then press 2.
steps.detail: The browser moves to workspace two and you go with it.
steps.completionMessage: The browser is on workspace two; the terminal stays on workspace one.

steps.instruction: Press Super and 1 to return to the terminal's workspace.
steps.completionMessage: And there's the terminal, right where you left it.

steps.instruction: Done with the terminal for now. Press Super and W.
steps.completionMessage: Closed. One more to go.

steps.instruction: Press Super and 2 to head over to the browser.
steps.completionMessage: There it is.

steps.instruction: And close it. Press Super and W.
steps.completionMessage: Both practice windows are closed.
